title: Uncertainties
examples: What is the difference between random and systematic error?
How do I calculate the percentage uncertainty for a measurement?
If my readings are always too high, what kind of error is that?

explain.say: Today we learn about measurement uncertainties in physics. Sometimes our measurements are not perfect. We must understand what makes them uncertain.
Some errors come from random fluctuations in the readings. These are random errors. They change unpredictably each time you measure something.
Other errors come from faulty equipment or technique. These are systematic errors. They consistently push your results in one direction.
Precision means how close repeated measurements are to each other. Accuracy means how close the measurement is to the true value.
For example, if you measure a length three times, getting 10.1 cm, 10.2 cm, and 10.1 cm, that is precise. But it might not be accurate.

faq.q: What is the difference between random and systematic error?
faq.a: Random errors are unpredictable variations in measurements. Systematic errors are consistent deviations from the true value, often due to faulty equipment.
asks: How do I spot a random error?
What causes systematic errors in physics?

faq.q: If my results are very close together, am I precise?
faq.a: Yes, if your repeated measurements cluster closely together, you are showing good precision. Precision only talks about the spread of your data points.
asks: What does it mean to be precise in science?

faq.q: How do I calculate the percentage uncertainty?
faq.a: You find the maximum absolute uncertainty first. Then you divide that by the measured value and multiply by one hundred percent.
asks: What is the formula for percent uncertainty?
Show me how to calculate percent uncertainty.

faq.q: Can I have both high precision and high accuracy?
faq.a: Yes, ideally, you want both high precision and high accuracy in your measurements. This means your data is close to each other and close to the true value.
asks: Is it possible to be accurate and precise?
What is the best outcome for measurements?

faq.q: Why is the least count important when calculating uncertainty?
faq.a: The least count gives you the smallest measurement you can reliably make with your instrument. This sets the initial estimate for your uncertainty.
asks: What is the uncertainty based on?
How does the instrument affect the uncertainty?

facts: Random errors change unpredictably from one reading to the next.
Systematic errors cause a consistent offset in all measurements.
Precision describes the closeness of repeated measurements to each other.
Accuracy describes how close a measurement is to the accepted true value.

quiz.say: A student measures a wire length as 10.0 cm, 10.1 cm, and 10.0 cm. This demonstrates:
quiz.why: The readings are very close to each other, showing good precision.

wrong.0: Random error suggests large, unpredictable swings between readings.
wrong.2: Accuracy depends on the true value, which we do not know here.
wrong.3: Systematic error implies a consistent bias, which is not evident here.

quiz.say: If a thermometer always reads two degrees too low, this is an example of:
quiz.why: The error is consistent, always being two degrees too low.

wrong.0: While it is inaccurate, 'systematic error' identifies the cause of the consistent inaccuracy.
wrong.2: Random error would cause the reading to jump up and down unpredictably.
wrong.3: Low precision means the readings are spread out, not consistently low.

quiz.say: A measurement of 50 plus or minus 2 percent uncertainty is written as:
quiz.why: The format for reporting a value with percentage uncertainty is the value followed by plus or minus the percentage.

wrong.1: This phrase is incomplete; it needs the uncertainty value written with the symbol.
wrong.2: Division is not the correct mathematical operation for reporting uncertainty.
wrong.3: Multiplication is incorrect; we use plus or minus to show the range of uncertainty.
